title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
summary: Compile after delivery means the payload arrives as source code or an intermediate form rather than as a finished executable, and the target system builds it before running it. Text files, scripts, and bytecode are far less likely to be flagged than a binary, because many controls and reviewers concentrate on executable formats. The build usually relies on tools already present on the host, such as the .NET compilers or the GNU compiler collection, and sometimes a compiler is bundled with the delivery itself. The compiled output may be written to disk and executed, or loaded directly into memory, which removes a file artefact entirely. Defenders hunt for development tooling running on production hosts, compiler processes started by office applications or script interpreters, and new executables created in temporary or user-writable directories.

beginner.definition: Normally, a program arrives on your computer ready to run. Compile after delivery means the attacker sends written instructions instead. The victim computer turns those instructions into a working program. Then it runs that program right there on the target machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools often look for finished program files, because those are what run. Plain text instructions look harmless and often pass these checks. The attacker can change the text easily without building anything new. If you do not watch for building tools, this step happens without notice.
howItWorks: The attacker writes the payload as source code or another unbuilt form.
They hide that text inside a document, an archive, or an encoded block.
The victim opens the file, and a small script unpacks the source and saves it.
A building tool already on the computer, such as a compiler, turns the source into a program.
The new program is written to a folder or loaded straight into memory and started.
Because the finished program was never delivered, delivery checks may see nothing wrong.
beginner.example: Imagine ordering a bookshelf that arrives as a flat pack. The shop never ships a finished shelf, so nothing looks like furniture. You build it yourself in your own living room. Compiling a payload after delivery is the same idea. The attacker ships the pieces, and your computer builds the harmful program.
takeaways: Attackers may deliver source code and build it on the target to avoid binary checks.
Compiler and build tools running on ordinary workstations are a strong warning sign.
Newly created programs in temporary or user folders deserve a closer look.

objectives: Explain what compiling after delivery means and why attackers use it.
Describe the common ways source code is delivered and hidden.
Identify native build tools that attackers reuse on a target host.
Explain how in-memory compilation avoids leaving an executable on disk.
Describe how to spot building activity on systems that should never build software.
